title: Proclamation and the duty to know the law
bodyMd:
In the cities of late medieval Italy a new ordinance did not, for practical purposes, exist until it had been cried. A herald read it aloud at the customary stations of the town — the steps of the main church, the gate of the market, the bridge where the dyers worked — and a notary wrote in the margin of the register the day, the hour and the stations at which each reading had taken place. In litigation that marginal note could matter more than the ordinance itself. A citizen charged with breaking a rule might escape the penalty altogether by showing that it had never been cried in his quarter.

The maxim that ignorance of the law excuses no one sat comfortably with this arrangement, because under it the maxim was very nearly true. The authority that wished to bind its subjects bore the burden of telling them, and the herald's rounds were the proof that it had done so. Ignorance was not excused because, in principle, it had been made impossible.

The spread of printed and posted edicts in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries is usually told as a story of improvement: more copies, a fixed wording, no dependence on a herald's voice or memory. All of that is true, but something else changed as well. A posted edict could be read by anyone who passed it; it no longer came to find the citizen, and the citizen had to go and find it. Courts in several states began to accept a single copy fixed to the door of the town hall as notice to the whole city, and the margins of the registers, once crowded with hours and places, shrank to a single line.

The maxim kept its wording but not its meaning. What had described a world in which the law was carried to every door became a rule about who must bear the cost when it was not. The burden of knowing the law had passed, almost without comment, from those who made it to those who had to obey it.
accessibilityText: A four-paragraph legal-history passage of about 340 words on how laws were made known. The first paragraph describes late medieval Italian cities, where a new ordinance was read aloud by a herald at customary stations of the town, such as the church steps, the market gate and the dyers' bridge, and a notary recorded in the register margin the day, hour and stations of each reading; in litigation that note could matter more than the ordinance, and a citizen could escape a penalty by showing that the rule had never been cried in his quarter. The second paragraph says the maxim that ignorance of the law excuses no one fitted this arrangement because it was then very nearly true: the authority bore the burden of telling its subjects, and the herald's rounds proved it had done so, so ignorance was in principle made impossible. The third paragraph says the spread of printed and posted edicts in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries is usually told as a story of improvement, with more copies, fixed wording and no dependence on a herald, and that this is true, but that something else changed: a posted edict no longer came to find the citizen, the citizen had to go and find it; courts in several states accepted one copy on the town-hall door as notice to the whole city, and the register margins shrank to a single line. The fourth paragraph concludes that the maxim kept its wording but not its meaning: from describing a world where the law reached every door it became a rule about who bears the cost when it does not, and the burden of knowing the law passed, almost without comment, from lawmakers to those who must obey.

provenance.notes: Original prose written for this question bank. The general practice of proclaiming laws aloud is historical background; the argument, the stations, the register detail and the wording are invented for this item set, and no published history, article or passage was copied, paraphrased or reconstructed.
